title: Sharp Tilting Inequalities
abstract: For positive semidefinite matrices $A,B$ and $1/2\leα\le1$, we establish $\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[A\,D\log(A^α+B^α)(B^α)\right] \le s^s(1-s)^{1-s}\operatorname{Tr}[A^αB^{1-α}]$, where $s=(1-α)/α$, with the optimal coefficient. The proof uses a superoperator representation of the directional derivative of the logarithm and an Araki-type estimate for the derivative of a fractional power. Both this inequality and its symmetric-quotient counterpart extend to positive trace-class $A$ and positive, possibly unbounded, self-adjoint $B$ on a separable Hilbert space.
summary: This paper derives and proves sharp trace inequalities, known as Sharp Tilting Inequalities, for positive semidefinite operators $A$ and $B$. It employs sophisticated techniques from functional calculus and superoperator theory to extend these results from finite matrices to general unbounded operators on Hilbert spaces. These inequalities are crucial mathematical tools for bounding quantities in quantum information theory and operator theory.
main_problem: The paper focuses on establishing and extending sharp trace inequalities, specifically 'Sharp Tilting Inequalities,' for positive semidefinite matrices and operators.
main_result: The core result is the inequality $\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[A\,D\log(A^\alpha+B^\alpha)(B^\alpha)ight] \le s^s(1-s)^{1-s}\operatorname{Tr}[A^\alphaB^{1-\alpha}]$, which is shown to hold for general trace-class and bounded operators.
method: The proof relies heavily on advanced operator calculus, including superoperator representations for directional derivatives of the logarithm and specialized Araki-type estimates for fractional power derivatives.
model_or_system: The mathematical framework involves abstract positive semidefinite matrices $A$ and $B$, which are generalized to self-adjoint operators on a separable Hilbert space. The context is purely mathematical operator theory applied to quantum observables.

paper_structure: The paper develops the argument by first proving the inequality for matrices (Theorem 4), then extending it to the symmetric quotient form (Proposition 5), and finally generalizing both results to the infinite-dimensional setting using spectral calculus and integral definitions (Theorem 6).
